lines.text: Imagine a spaceship with no engine and no fuel, that never stops speeding up.
You and I are going to fly one, powered by nothing but sunlight.
Here's the weird part: light has no mass, but it still carries momentum.
When a photon hits a mirror, it bounces off and gives it a tiny shove.
Bounce it straight back? Double the kick!
On real sails, that push is less than the weight of a paperclip.
But space has no friction, and the Sun never switches off, so your speed just keeps building.
And this idea is old! Four centuries ago, Kepler saw comet tails point away from the Sun, and guessed sunlight was pushing them.
In the 1870s, Maxwell predicted light really does push, and around 1900, physicists measured it.
In 2010, a Japanese probe called Ikaros unfurled a sail on its way to Venus, and flew on sunlight.
Now scientists have proposed tiny probes on sails, pushed by giant lasers,
fast enough to reach the nearest stars in about twenty years. At Voyager's speed? Tens of thousands.
Light, the same stuff warming your face right now, could one day carry us to another star.
